title: The Menu
author: VirtueVigil Editorial Team

woke_trap_assessment.explanation: Margin is positive (barely). Not a woke trap. The film's class warfare satire is front and center within the first fifteen minutes. There is no bait-and-switch. Conservative viewers will know exactly what they are dealing with well before the halfway point.

director.name: Mark Mylod
director.ideology: CENTER-LEFT. Primarily a television director known for Succession and Game of Thrones. His sensibility is satirical, dark, and class-conscious without being overtly political. He does not moralize; he observes and then burns things down.
director.profile: British director Mark Mylod built his reputation directing prestige television, most notably Succession (multiple Emmy awards) and Game of Thrones. The Menu is his most prominent theatrical feature. His background in Succession is evident throughout: the same razor-sharp class observation, the same black humor about wealthy people trapped in systems of their own making, the same preference for letting characters damn themselves rather than delivering moral lectures. Mylod is a craftsman first and an ideologue never. His instincts align more with social satire than political messaging. The film's visual control, tight 107-minute runtime, and willingness to withhold easy resolution all reflect his television background elevated to theatrical ambition.

writers.profile: Seth Reiss and Will Tracy met writing for The Onion and Late Night with Seth Meyers. Tracy also wrote White Noise (2022) for Noah Baumbach. Their background in satirical comedy shapes the film's tone: it is designed to be funny and unsettling simultaneously, never earnest about its class critique. The script is disciplined in a way that pure ideology rarely is. It finds its themes through character logic rather than statement. Margot's eventual escape via the cheeseburger is not a political lesson; it is a character beat that happens to carry meaning. That distinction matters.

lead_producer.name: Adam McKay, Betsy Koch, Will Ferrell
lead_producer.company: Hyperobject Industries / Gary Sanchez Productions / Searchlight Pictures

composer.name: Colin Stetson
composer.profile: Experimental musician and composer known for intense, unnerving work. His score for The Menu relies on discordant tones and deliberate tension-building. It refuses to comfort the audience when they want it.

top_cast.name: Ralph Fiennes
top_cast.notes: The film is built around Fiennes' performance and it earns every second of his screen time. Slowik is frightening not because he is manic but because he is completely calm. He has made peace with his own darkness. Fiennes plays him with a stillness that is more disturbing than any amount of screaming could be. His earlier ease and later collapse into nihilism are both utterly convincing. Golden Globe nominated.

top_cast.name: Anya Taylor-Joy
top_cast.notes: The moral center of the film and its only character with real survival instinct. Taylor-Joy plays Margot as perceptive and pragmatic: she is the only guest who sees Slowik clearly because she is the only one without something to prove. Her cheeseburger scene is the film's best moment, and she plays it with perfect low-key wit.

top_cast.name: Nicholas Hoult
top_cast.notes: Plays the film's most contemptible character: a food obsessive so invested in the mythology of Chef Slowik that he knowingly escorts a woman to her death for the experience. Hoult makes Tyler pathetic rather than monstrous, which is the harder and more interesting choice. His kitchen humiliation scene is brutal.

top_cast.name: Janet McTeer
top_cast.notes: The film reserves special venom for the critical class, and McTeer's performance earns it. Lillian is the kind of powerful critic who has turned her personal taste into institutional authority. She is fascinating and awful in equal measure.

fidelityCasting.assessment: The Menu is an original production with no source adaptation to evaluate. The casting is largely accurate to the script's intentions. Anya Taylor-Joy was cast specifically because her unconventional look reinforced Margot's status as someone who does not belong in this world. Ralph Fiennes embodies the creative-genius-turned-nihilist archetype without relying on obvious menace cues.

parentalGuidance.parentalNotes: This is a hard R film intended for adults. The violence is precise and shocking rather than gratuitous, but it is genuinely disturbing. Not appropriate for children or younger teens. Conservative families should be aware that the film contains a sympathetic escort character and depicts sexual harassment explicitly. The satire targets elites across the political spectrum.

summary.overall:
The Menu is a slick, well-crafted class satire that will make you laugh and make you uneasy, sometimes at the same time. It is also a film whose ideological message is more muddled than its admirers want to admit.

The setup is elegant. A group of wealthy diners travel to a remote island restaurant run by celebrity chef Julian Slowik (Ralph Fiennes, terrifying and still). Over the course of the evening, Slowik reveals that the menu has a purpose beyond food: each guest is there to be punished for what they represent. The film makes them all complicit in something. The food critic who destroyed careers with her reviews. The wealthy regulars who treated the restaurant as a symbol of their status. The tech bros who exploit other people's work. The faded movie star coasting on name recognition. And Tyler, the food obsessive who brought his date knowing she would die, because the experience was worth more to him than she was.

Only Margot (Anya Taylor-Joy) escapes, and the reason she escapes is the film's thesis statement. She orders a cheeseburger. Not because she is clever about it but because she is hungry and the food she has been served is, in her direct assessment, 'loveless.' Slowik finds joy in making it. A real thing, made with real care, for a real person. The pretension falls away. The artifice collapses. The cheeseburger saves her life.

There is something genuinely conservative in that message, and I mean that as a compliment. The film has contempt for the people who have elevated food (and by extension, art, culture, entertainment) into a status competition so abstract it has lost all connection to the thing itself. The food critic destroys chefs for sport. The foodie Tyler cannot taste anymore; he can only evaluate. The wealthy diners do not eat; they perform. The film is savagely funny about all of this, and its contempt feels earned rather than cheap.

But. The film also frames Slowik's rampage as a kind of labor uprising. He had his passion destroyed by the consumer class. His staff follow him into death with cultish devotion because he is the only person who ever saw them as skilled workers rather than service employees. The anti-capitalist reading is available, and the film does not work hard to prevent you from taking it.

This is what pushes the score to MIXED rather than TRADITIONAL LEAN. The film critiques both the consumer class and the artist class. It celebrates authenticity over pretension. But it also positions the service and creative worker as exploited victims of a rigged economic system. Both critiques are present and neither one fully wins.

Ralph Fiennes is extraordinary. He is genuinely frightening in a role that could easily tip into camp. Anya Taylor-Joy is the best she has been in a long time. The film is 107 minutes and does not waste a single one.

The question for conservative viewers is: can you enjoy a darkly funny film about wealthy people getting what they deserve, even if the economic framing occasionally tilts left? If the answer is yes, The Menu is one of the more sharply crafted genre films of 2022. If you need your entertainment to be ideologically tidy, look elsewhere.
summary.oneLiner: A masterfully crafted class satire where the cheeseburger is the conservative hero and the food critics deserve everything they get. Brilliant filmmaking, mixed message.
summary.verdict: The Menu's contempt for cultural pretension and status-obsessed elites plays as conservative instinct. The anti-capitalist undercurrent muddies the waters. Ralph Fiennes is one of the best performances of 2022. Worth watching.
summary.adultInsight: Conservative adults will find much to enjoy in The Menu's savaging of pretentious cultural elites. The film's core argument, that authenticity and directness defeat artifice every time, aligns with traditional values. The economic framing occasionally veers left. But Mylod is too sharp a director to let ideology overwhelm craft. Watch it for Fiennes and Taylor-Joy. Think about it for the cheeseburger.
summary.parentalGuidance: Hard R. Adults only. Strong violence, disturbing content, sexual references. Not appropriate for children or teens.

tropeAudit.name: Class Warfare Anti-Capitalist Satire
tropeAudit.description: The film's central engine is class resentment directed upward. Slowik punishes the consumer class, the investor class, and the celebrity class for destroying his passion for craft. His staff function as an organized labor force who follow him into collective death rather than continue serving the wealthy. The anti-capitalist reading is available and the script invites it. Producer Adam McKay (The Big Short, Don't Look Up) is a committed left-wing satirist whose fingerprints are on the film's political sensibility.

tropeAudit.name: Toxic Masculinity / Male Ego Critique
tropeAudit.description: Tyler's obsessive foodie culture and his willingness to sacrifice Margot for an experience are framed as the logical endpoint of a particular kind of male ego. Slowik's loss of passion is also partly attributed to male pride and the inability to accept limitations. Neither critique is sustained or explicit, but the film returns to male ego as a form of corruption multiple times.

tropeAudit.name: Sexual Harassment Addressed / Male Abuser Consequences
tropeAudit.description: Slowik allows himself to be stabbed by Katherine, an employee he sexually harassed. The scene is handled with minimal drama: Slowik presents his own punishment as part of the menu. The #MeToo resonance is clear but not heavy-handed. The film is not primarily about this; it is one note in a larger chord.

tropeAudit.name: Authenticity Over Pretension / Cheeseburger as Truth
tropeAudit.description: Margot escapes because she asks for something real. A cheeseburger. Not the elaborate symbolic dish Slowik has prepared to make a point, but actual food made with care for an actual hungry person. Slowik responds to it because it strips away the performance and returns to the original thing: a cook making food for someone who wants to eat it. This is a deeply traditional insight. The film's climax rewards directness, simplicity, and the refusal to participate in elite cultural performance.

tropeAudit.name: Elite Cultural Class Savaged / Critics and Elites Punished
tropeAudit.description: The film reserves its most sustained contempt for the food critic Lillian Bloom, whose entire career is framed as parasitic destruction of creative work she cannot match. The wealthy regulars are shown as status-seekers with no relationship to the actual food. The tech bros are oblivious and cruel. This is not a left-wing critique of capitalism; it is a very old critique of the corrupt cultural establishment that pretends to judge merit while serving its own interests.

tropeAudit.name: Common Sense / Working Class Pragmatism Rewarded
tropeAudit.description: Margot is not the smartest character in the film and not the bravest. She survives because she is pragmatic. She does not play the game. She does not perform sophistication she does not feel. She asks for what she actually wants and is honest about who she is when pressed. In a film full of people performing cultural sophistication, her refusal to perform is treated as the only authentic act. The film rewards working-class directness over elite pretension.

detailed_analysis:
The Menu is a film that conservative critics have largely misread. They see the anti-capitalist messaging and dismiss it. They miss the cheeseburger.

The film's thesis is actually quite old and quite traditional: authenticity defeats performance. Margot survives not because she is ideologically correct but because she is real. She does not pretend to be something she is not. She does not participate in Slowik's performance. She asks for what she actually wants.

This is why the film is MIXED rather than WOKE. Both the class critique and the authenticity-over-pretension message are present and neither fully wins. The film is content to hold both simultaneously.

For conservative viewers, the practical question is whether you can extract value from a film whose economic framing occasionally tilts left. The answer should be yes. The Menu's contempt for the critical class, for cultural status performance, and for the parasitic relationship between wealthy consumers and working artists is sharp and funny and earned. Ralph Fiennes gives one of the great villain performances of the decade.
